(CNN)  -- Manny Pacquiao's two-round demolition of Ricky Hatton has set up the prospect of the biggest money-spinning fight in the history of boxing. Pacquiao lands a solid right to Hatton on his way to a comprehensive victory. The Filipino knocked out the plucky but outclassed Briton in Las Vegas on Saturday night -- earning him by a conservative estimate at least $2 million dollars per minute. Hatton, who could well now hang up his gloves, will pocket more than $8 million as a consolation. Pacquiao's all-action style is popular with boxing followers and in his native Philippines the theaters which screened his fight live with Hatton were sold out well in advance with a ferocious demand for tickets. But the really big money lies in the Pay Per View (PPV) revenues generated by the U.S. Home Box Office (HBO) network. USA Today reported Monday that early indications from cable companies were that the scheduled 12-round light-welterweight bout could get as many as two million buys. Co-promoter Bob Arum was delighted with the figures especially as initial estimates were suggesting about one million boxing fans would shell out their cash. "We know based on those early numbers and based on experience the event will perform extremely well. If I had to guess, anywhere between 1.6 million and two million homes, which is a home run," he said. The record for a PPV event is the 2.4 million buys for 'Golden Boy' Oscar De La Hoya's May 2007 fight with Floyd Mayweather Jr., which generated a staggering $134 million in revenue. Mayweather, who also beat Hatton in another 'superfight' at the back end of 2007, astutely chose Saturday night in Vegas to announce he was coming out of retirement. Mayweather, nicknamed 'money' because of the enormous revenues he generates, will face Mexico's Juan Manuel Marquez on July 18 in his return to the ring. But the talk of the boxing world is an eventual match up against Pacquiao with the notional pound for pound title at stake as well as a massive pay day. "If Mayweather wants a piece of the 'little Filipino', just be my guest," Arum said before the dust had barely settled on the Hatton fight. With the flamboyant De La Hoya retired after being handed a painful beating by Pacquiao at the back end of 2008, the mantle of PPV king is set to fall to one of the two men who ended his ring career. Despite the global recession, the appetite for top prize fighting remains strong, but it is the more flamboyant characters who draw the biggest audiences. Last November's HBO clash between former pound for pound champion Roy Jones Jr. and the brilliant undefeated Welsh world champion Joe Calzaghe drew less than 250,000 buys. The only potential obstacle to a Pacquiao-Mayweather bout, the dangerous Marquez aside, is the relative sizes of the two men. Mayweather is a natural welterweight and would want a fight at 147 pounds, with Pacquiao, who started his remarkable career at light-flyweight, wanting the match at a lower weight. But big business and money is set to talk and many predict the showdown will come late this year, almost certainly in Las Vegas.

(CNN) -- Manny Pacquiao’s two-round demolition of Ricky Hatton has raised the prospect of the most lucrative fight in boxing history.

Pacquiao landed a solid right hand on Hatton en route to a comprehensive victory. The Filipino knocked out the courageous but outclassed Briton in Las Vegas on Saturday night, earning, by conservative estimates, at least $2 million per minute. Hatton, who may now choose to hang up his gloves, will receive more than $8 million in consolation.

Pacquiao’s all-action style has made him immensely popular among boxing fans, and in his native Philippines, theaters screening his fight with Hatton live were sold out well in advance amid fierce demand for tickets.

Yet the truly significant money lies in the Pay-Per-View (PPV) revenue generated by the U.S. Home Box Office (HBO) network. USA Today reported Monday that early indications from cable companies suggested the scheduled 12-round light-welterweight bout could attract as many as two million buys.

Co-promoter Bob Arum was delighted with the figures, particularly as initial estimates had suggested that about one million boxing fans would pay to watch the fight.

“We know based on those early numbers and based on experience the event will perform extremely well. If I had to guess, anywhere between 1.6 million and two million homes, which is a home run,” he said.

The record for a PPV event stands at 2.4 million buys for “Golden Boy” Oscar De La Hoya’s May 2007 fight with Floyd Mayweather Jr., which generated a staggering $134 million in revenue.

Mayweather, who also defeated Hatton in another “superfight” late in 2007, astutely chose Saturday night in Las Vegas to announce his return from retirement.

Mayweather, nicknamed “Money” because of the enormous revenues he generates, will face Mexico’s Juan Manuel Marquez on July 18 in his comeback fight.

However, the boxing world is already focused on a potential showdown with Pacquiao, with the notional pound-for-pound title at stake alongside a massive payday.

“If Mayweather wants a piece of the ‘little Filipino,’ just be my guest,” Arum said before the dust had barely settled on the Hatton fight.

With the flamboyant De La Hoya now retired after absorbing a painful beating from Pacquiao late in 2008, the mantle of PPV king appears set to pass to one of the two men who ended his ring career.

Despite the global recession, appetite for elite prizefighting remains strong, though it is the more flamboyant personalities who draw the largest audiences. Last November’s HBO clash between former pound-for-pound champion Roy Jones Jr. and the brilliant, undefeated Welsh world champion Joe Calzaghe drew fewer than 250,000 buys.

The only potential obstacle to a Pacquiao-Mayweather bout, aside from the dangerous Marquez, is the difference in size between the two fighters. Mayweather is a natural welterweight and would want the fight at 147 pounds, while Pacquiao, who began his remarkable career at light-flyweight, would prefer the match at a lower weight.

But big business and money are likely to prevail, and many predict the showdown will take place late this year, almost certainly in Las Vegas.

(CNN) — Manny Pacquiao’s crushing two-round victory over Ricky Hatton has opened the door to what could become the most lucrative bout boxing has ever seen.

Pacquiao landed a heavy right hand on Hatton during a dominant performance that ended with the Filipino star knocking out the brave but overmatched British fighter in Las Vegas on Saturday night. By cautious calculations, Pacquiao earned at least $2 million for every minute he spent in the ring. Hatton, who may now decide to retire from boxing, is still expected to receive more than $8 million.

Pacquiao’s aggressive, action-packed approach has made him a favorite among fight fans. In his home country of the Philippines, cinemas showing the Hatton fight live had sold out long before the event, with demand for seats extremely high.

The largest financial rewards, however, come from U.S. pay-per-view sales through the HBO network. USA Today reported Monday that preliminary feedback from cable providers suggested the scheduled 12-round light-welterweight fight might attract up to two million purchases.

Bob Arum, one of the event’s co-promoters, was thrilled by the numbers, particularly because early projections had pointed to roughly one million paying viewers.

“Based on those early figures and our experience, we know the event is going to do extremely well. If I had to estimate, I’d say somewhere between 1.6 million and two million homes, which is a home run,” Arum said.

The all-time pay-per-view record belongs to Oscar “Golden Boy” De La Hoya’s May 2007 bout with Floyd Mayweather Jr., which drew 2.4 million buys and produced an extraordinary $134 million in revenue.

Mayweather, who also defeated Hatton in a major fight near the end of 2007, used Saturday night in Las Vegas to cleverly announce that he was ending his retirement. Known as “Money” because of the huge income his fights generate, Mayweather is scheduled to return to the ring on July 18 against Mexico’s Juan Manuel Marquez.

Still, the fight everyone in boxing is now discussing is a future showdown between Mayweather and Pacquiao, with both the unofficial pound-for-pound crown and an enormous payday on the line.

“If Mayweather wants a piece of the ‘little Filipino,’ he’s welcome to try,” Arum said shortly after the Hatton fight had ended.

With the showy De La Hoya now retired following the punishing loss Pacquiao handed him late in 2008, the title of pay-per-view king appears likely to pass to one of the two fighters who brought De La Hoya’s career to a close.

Even during the worldwide economic downturn, demand remains high for major prizefights. However, the biggest audiences tend to be drawn by the sport’s most colorful personalities. By comparison, last November’s HBO fight between former pound-for-pound leader Roy Jones Jr. and unbeaten Welsh world champion Joe Calzaghe brought in fewer than 250,000 pay-per-view buys.

Apart from the threat posed by Marquez, the main possible complication in making a Pacquiao-Mayweather fight is the difference in their natural sizes. Mayweather is naturally a welterweight and would prefer to fight at 147 pounds, while Pacquiao, who began his remarkable professional career as a light-flyweight, would want the contest held at a lower weight.

Even so, the influence of business and money is expected to be decisive. Many observers believe the matchup will take place late this year, almost certainly in Las Vegas.

He defeated Hatton more decisively than Mayweather had in 2007, when Mayweather stopped Hatton in the 10th round. Comparisons were inevitable. Pacquiao’s explosive performance strengthened the argument that he was the one fighter capable of challenging Mayweather’s claim as the best boxer of his era.

From a financial standpoint, the timing could not have been better. Mayweather, unbeaten and still regarded by many as the sport’s finest technician, remained one of boxing’s biggest pay-per-view draws. Pacquiao, meanwhile, had become a global phenomenon, carrying the support of the Philippines and attracting a rapidly growing international audience. His wins over Oscar De La Hoya and Hatton proved that he was no longer merely a great fighter moving up in weight — he was a mainstream boxing superstar.

A Pacquiao-Mayweather fight offered the rare combination promoters crave: elite talent, contrasting styles, undefeated mystique versus relentless ambition, and enormous fan bases on both sides. Mayweather’s defensive brilliance and counterpunching mastery would be matched against Pacquiao’s ferocious pace, southpaw attack and unorthodox movement. Beyond the sporting intrigue, the commercial appeal was obvious. It had all the ingredients to break pay-per-view records and become the richest fight in boxing history.

Pacquiao’s destruction of Hatton effectively removed one of the final barriers to that possibility. He had proven he could carry his power to higher weights, defeat elite names, and generate massive interest in major events. With Mayweather returning to the spotlight and Pacquiao at the peak of his popularity, the public appetite for a meeting between them became impossible to ignore.

In beating Hatton so spectacularly, Pacquiao did not simply win another title fight. He created the conditions for boxing’s ultimate prizefight — a global event against Mayweather that promised unprecedented revenue, historic stakes and a definitive answer to the question of who was the greatest fighter of their generation.
